summary: The English of the six mishnayot is close and brief, and the rulings on the commentary are accurate. The main faults: 1:17 renders 'nothing better than silence' (Rabbeinu Yonah's variant, not the base אֶלָּא) and 'study' for מִדְרָשׁ against Bartenura and Rambam, who read it as expounding; the Zechariah verse in 1:18 cuts off the objects of שִׁפְטוּ; and the 1:13 grammar note derives יָסֵף from יסף 'add', which Bartenura's gloss יָסוּף rules out. Many senses were filled mechanically or point to the wrong homograph (place names Azem and Tob, 'father' for מֵבִיא, 'unit of measure' for gates), and the morphology has a few wrong analyses (אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ is a perfect, מִשְׁפַּט is construct, gender of קְטָלָא and אֹמֶד, the Aramaic lemmas in 1:13).

patches.value: He used to say: One who spreads his name far loses his name; and one who does not add will cease; and one who does not learn deserves to die; and one who makes use of the crown passes away.
patches.reason: נָגֵד is 'draw out, stretch'; Bartenura: מִי שֶׁנִּמְשַׁךְ שְׁמוֹ לְמֵרָחוֹק, one whose name is drawn out far. 'Makes a name great' loses the image of the name stretched afar, which the token gloss and the phrase literal already give.

value.english: One who spreads his name far loses his name
value.literal: 'one who draws out a name, his name is lost'; נגד as extending a name far through rank and lordship, Bartenura

value.english: and one who does not add will cease
value.literal: 'and who not adds, will cease'; Bartenura: does not add to his learning, so what he has learned ceases from him

value.english: and one who does not learn deserves to die
value.literal: 'and who not learns, death liable'; Bartenura: it is fitting that he be killed

value.english: and one who makes use of the crown passes away
value.literal: 'and who uses the crown, passes'; the crown is the crown of Torah, Bartenura

patches.reason: the new English changed the first saying's fragment
periphrastic הָיָה אוֹמֵר is 'he was (saying)': Qal 'to be' (1.1.3), not 1.1.1.1 'to happen, come to pass'.
מוֹסִיף is a Hif'il (Af'el) participle; the matching sense is the Hiphil 'add, increase' (1.3.1), not the stem-less head sense.

יָסֵף is not from יסף 'add': Bartenura glosses it יָסוּף, 'will come to an end' (root סוף), and his alternative is יֵאָסֵף (root אסף). The pack's bdbs:יָסַף 'to add' is the wrong lexeme and lists no other entry, so the sense is removed (see the note and the morph patch).

patches.value: Aramaic imperfect; Bartenura reads it as יָסוּף, from סוף 'come to an end': what he has learned will cease from his mouth. It is not the root of מוֹסִיף (יסף 'add'); the two words make a sound-play. The pack's lexicon entry (bdbs:יָסַף 'add') is the wrong lexeme, so no sense is given. Vilna reads יסיף.
patches.reason: the old note left the word under יסף 'add'; the lexicon entry does not fit the word and the sense is removed.
the brief asks for a sense on every noun whose entry lists senses; jastrow:קְטָלָא 1 'killing, death-penalty' is the sense here.
jastrow:שָׁמַשׁ 2 is 'to minister, officiate'; the reflexive with ב, 'to make use of', is 5.1 (Nithpa., 'with ב ... of persons, to make use of').

patches.value: Aramaic Ithpa'el perfect of שמש, אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ (from אִתְשַׁמֵּשׁ, the ת and שׁ change places), 'has made use of'; after דְּ it makes a general relative clause, 'whoever makes use of'. With ב: 'make use of a thing'.
patches.reason: the form is a perfect, not a participle (the Ithpa'el participle is מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ, as in Bartenura's gloss הַמִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ), and the stem is Ithpa'el, not Ittaf'al.

value: This saying is in Aramaic, except for the opening formula הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר; the Aramaic relative is דְּ- (Hebrew שֶׁ-) and the emphatic ending is -ָא (שְׁמָא, קְטָלָא, תָּגָא).

Four short clauses, each a relative clause (a participle in the first three, the perfect אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ in the last) followed by its consequence; the first and the last are an inverted pair (name drawn out, name lost; crown used, one passes).

וּדְלֹא מוֹסִיף יָסֵף: a sound-play between two roots, מוֹסִיף from יסף 'add' and יָסֵף, which Bartenura reads as יָסוּף from סוף 'come to an end' (or, in his second reading, יֵאָסֵף 'be gathered (to his people)', from אסף): 'who does not add will cease'.
קְטָלָא חַיָּב: the adjective חַיָּב is predicate with the noun it governs, 'liable (to) death'.
patches.reason: the note said that 'add' and 'come to an end' are both the root יסף; they are not (סוף 'end', אסף 'gather'), and Bartenura's gloss יָסוּף shows the root. The note also called the last clause a participle clause; אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ is a perfect.

morphemes.parse: qal, participle active, masculine, singular, absolute

patches.reason: נָגֵד here is the Aramaic verb נְגַד 'to draw, drag, stretch' (Bartenura: לְשׁוֹן מְשִׁיכָה, Targum מִשְׁכוּ = נְגִידוּ). The lemma נָגַד is the Hebrew verb ('draw a line'; Hif. 'tell'), a different lexeme; the Aramaic Pe'al perfect is נְגַד.

שְׁמָא is the emphatic (determined) state; the brief's lemma is the singular absolute, which in Aramaic is שֻׁם (Biblical Aramaic, Ezra 5:1), the cognate of Hebrew שֵׁם. The pack found no entry for the lemma שְׁמָא.
same lexeme as 1:13.5: the lemma is the absolute שֻׁם, not the emphatic שְׁמָא; שְׁמֵהּ is the form before the 3ms suffix.

root and lemma: Bartenura glosses יָסֵף as יָסוּף 'will come to an end', root סוף (his alternative יֵאָסֵף is from אסף); neither reading is יסף 'add', which belongs only to מוֹסִיף. The lemma by the brief's rule is the Qal perfect of סוף, סָף. The parse (Pe'al/Qal imperfect 3ms) stands.
קְטָלָא is masculine (Jastrow: קְטָלָא (m.) 'killing, death-penalty'); the final -ָא is the Aramaic emphatic ending, not a feminine ending.
אִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ is the Ithpa'el perfect 3ms (prefix אִ-); the Ithpa'el participle would be מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ, as Bartenura paraphrases it. 'Participle active' is wrong.
periphrastic הָיָה אוֹמֵר: Qal 'to be' (1.1.3), not 'to happen' (1.1.1.1).

value: Three rhetorical questions, each with a conditional first half; the answer to each is understood.
אֵין אֲנִי לִי: אֵין negates the existence of the subject 'I' for the benefit 'to me'; the verbless clause has no verb 'to be'.

לִי comes twice in the same sense, 'for me': 'if I am not for me, who is for me?'. The English renders the first 'for myself' because its subject is also 'I'; לְעַצְמִי 'for my self' in the next clause sharpens it.
וּכְשֶׁאֲנִי לְעַצְמִי: כְּשֶׁ- is the Mishnaic 'when', compounded from כ + שֶׁ.
אֵימָתַי is the Mishnaic interrogative 'when', and עַכְשָׁיו the Mishnaic 'now'.
patches.reason: the note said לִי is used in two different senses; both are the same preposition with the same 1cs suffix and the same sense 'for me'. Only the English differs.

patches.value: Shimon his son says: All my days I grew up among the sages, and I have found nothing good for the body except silence. And it is not expounding that is the main thing, but action. And whoever multiplies words brings sin.
patches.reason: (1) The Hebrew is לֹא מָצָאתִי ... טוֹב אֶלָּא שְׁתִיקָה, 'I have not found (anything) good ... except silence': טוֹב is positive and אֶלָּא is 'except'. 'Nothing better ... than' renders the reading טוֹב מִשְּׁתִיקָה of Rabbeinu Yonah's lemma, not the base text. (2) Both normative commentators read מִדְרָשׁ as speech about Torah: Bartenura הַמִּדְרָשׁ וְהַדְּרָשׁ וְהַדִּבּוּר בַּתּוֹרָה, which is why it follows the praise of silence; Rambam 'that his deeds agree with his words', with דרוש ולך נאה לדרוש. 'Study' loses the link to speech; 'expounding' keeps it, as the translator's own token note says.

value: עַל שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים הָעוֹלָם עוֹמֵד: the preposition עַל means 'upon' (the world rests on); the participle עוֹמֵד is 'stands, endures'.
The three items are each introduced with עַל and the article: הַדִּין, הָאֱמֶת, הַשָּׁלוֹם.
שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר introduces the verse (Zech 8:16) as a proof text; the mishnah reads the verse as naming the three things, truth, judgment, and peace.
אֱמֶת וּמִשְׁפַּט שָׁלוֹם שִׁפְטוּ: the two nouns are the objects of the plural imperative שִׁפְטוּ 'judge', put before it for emphasis; מִשְׁפַּט is in the construct, 'a judgment of peace'.
בְּשַׁעֲרֵיכֶם: 'in your gates', the place of the court.
patches.reason: the note did not say that the nouns are the objects of שִׁפְטוּ, nor that מִשְׁפַּט is construct.
